articles.body: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivered his State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, 4 pm, at the Batasang Pambansa in Quezon City. The situation was markedly different from last year, when Marcos’ erstwhile ally, Vice President Sara Duterte, avoided an impeachment trial after the Supreme Court ruled that the complaint against her was unconstitutional as it is barred by the one-year rule. This year, as Marcos delivered his fifth SONA, the impeachment trial against the Vice President is in full swing. Leyte 1st District Representative Martin Romualdez, the President’s cousin, is no longer House speaker following his resignation after he was implicated in flood control corruption. Marcos himself had announced a crackdown on those involved in the scandal in his SONA last year. How will Marcos set the tone for the last two years of his presidency? What promises will he declare as fulfilled, and what remains to be done? What will be his new marching order a year since he called for a crackdown on flood control corruption? articles.title: SONA 2026: Marcos makes no mention of Sara Duterte impeachment trial
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The absence of any mention of Vice President Sara Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial in President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. ’s State of the Nation Address (SONA) drew mixed reactions from the prosecution team.
articles.body: MANILA, Philippines – The absence of any mention of Vice President Sara Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial in President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s State of the Nation Address (SONA) drew mixed reactions from the prosecution team. The televised speech, watched by millions of Filipinos, was formally addressed to Congress, where one chamber impeached Vice President Sara Duterte for a second time in May and the other will decide whether she should be convicted or acquitted. “We expected that it would be mentioned, so yes, we’re disappointed that it was not mentioned,” prosecution spokesperson Renee Co said, adding that Marcos could have at least asked Congress to respect the process and let the trial run its full course. House prosecutors Leila de Lima and Chel Diokno, however, said, Marcos’ exclusion of the ongoing trial in his speech did not come as a surprise. “I didn’t expect it. I think the administration has been consistent in terms of keeping their hands off the case,” Diokno said. “We were expecting that it won’t be mentioned, for him to show that he is hands off when it comes to impeachment,” Mamamayang Liberal Representative de Lima added. “But he could have still said something about the need for accountability. I hope he had at least one or two sentences about that.” Play Video Marcos, who has distanced himself from the impeachment efforts against the Vice President, said in early July that it would have been easier for the court if Duterte personally showed up at the trial. His son, House Majority Leader Sandro Marcos, denied involvement in the operations of the House prosecution. “They’re all brilliant in their own way. Let them do what they need to do,” the younger Marcos said ahead of his father’s SONA on Monday. Play Video One of the impeachment articles against the Vice President concerns her alleged threats against the lives of the President, First Lady Liza Marcos, and former House speaker Martin Romualdez. Duterte skipped Marcos’ SONA and said in an interview in The Hague that she had no plans of watching the speech . “I truly believe it is a waste of time of the Filipino people,” she said. While most of the 317 lawmakers were present on Monday, only 11 of the 24-member Senate attended the joint session at the Batasang Pambansa. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Another fuel price hike set for July 28
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – Pump prices are going up sharply again starting Tuesday, July 28, extending the run of fuel price increases driven by renewed volatility in the Middle East.
articles.body: MANILA, Philippines – Pump prices are going up sharply again starting Tuesday, July 28, extending the run of fuel price increases driven by renewed volatility in the Middle East. In a press conference on Tuesday, July 28, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin announced the following maximum price increases for the week of July 28 to August 3: Gasoline – increase of P6.80 per liter Diesel – increase of P7.32 per liter Kerosene – increase of P4.22 per liter The adjustments will take effect on Tuesday. “These price movements continue to stem from the developments in the Middle East, which have kept global oil markets under pressure. If there’s trouble in Ukraine or in the Strait of Hormuz, prices here are affected,” Garin said in a mix of English and Filipino. “This is how vulnerable we are.” Garin also said that fuel inventories remain “sufficient” at a “very healthy level” with no disruption to supply. There is a “glimmer of hope” that fuel prices could decline next week, according to Energy Undersecretary Sandy Sales. Progress in third-party negotiations, including the involvement of China and Pakistan, as well as the halt in missile strikes between Iran and the United States, helped pull down global oil prices in trading sessions on last Friday, July 24, and Monday, July 27. Before the latest adjustment, the Department of Energy’s (DOE) price monitoring showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P71.80 per liter for gasoline RON95, P70.30 per liter for gasoline RON91, P88.40 per liter for diesel, and P117 per liter for kerosene for the week of July 21 to 27. The latest increases follow last week’s bigtime fuel price hike s, when gasoline prices rose by P3.65 per liter, diesel by P10.68 per liter, and kerosene by P11.77 per liter. Diesel and kerosene prices sharply higher on July 21, dashing hopes that pump prices would soon return to levels seen before the Middle East conflict. Garin had said the increase was still being driven by uncertainty from tensions involving Iran, Israel, and the United States, which have continued to affect the global oil market. (READ: Iran war spreads to Red Sea and Caspian, Gulf quiet as US forgoes strikes ) Global oil prices have remained volatile as conflict in the Middle East continues to threaten key shipping routes. The Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman, remains one of the world’s most important oil shipping routes. Any disruption to tanker traffic can quickly affect global crude and refined product prices. That matters for the Philippines because the country imports much of its fuel as finished petroleum products, including diesel and gasoline. This means local pump prices are more directly influenced by regional traded prices of finished fuels, especially the Mean of Platts Singapore, or MOPS, rather than Dubai crude alone. Despite intermittent easing in crude prices, local pump prices remain well above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene. The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com Must Read [Vantage Point] Oil’s false prophets

articles.title: Land disputes stall Basilan road projects, leave farmers paying price
articles.summary: BASILAN, Philippines – Thousands of farmers and residents in Basilan continue to bear the cost of stalled infrastructure projects, with unfinished roads driving up transport expenses, disrupting access to markets, and isolating communities.
articles.body: BASILAN, Philippines – Thousands of farmers and residents in Basilan continue to bear the cost of stalled infrastructure projects, with unfinished roads driving up transport expenses, disrupting access to markets, and isolating communities. Nearly 100 road projects, mostly farm-to-market roads, remain stalled, unfinished, or suspended due to unresolved road right-of-way disputes, according to records from the Bangsamoro Ministry of Public Works. The ministry’s Basilan District Engineering Office this year secured a P627-million infrastructure program covering a road network across 11 municipalities of Basilan , including Lamitan City. A large portion of this year’s budget, as well as allocations from previous years, has been earmarked for farm-to-market roads intended to help farmers, fisherfolk, and consumers transport agricultural produce more efficiently to markets. But despite the regional government’s push to expand the road network of the province, nearly 70% of Basilan’s ongoing road projects have experienced “delays or project abandonment.” Some have remained unfinished for more than a year, while others have been delayed for several months. Acting District Engineer Alnaif Ronie Cuevas told Rappler that the delays stem from overlapping family inheritance disputes and informal tribal land systems. Cuevas said the biggest obstacle holding back these multimillion-peso contracts is the long-running problem of unresolved right-of-way disputes. In previous infrastructure projects, budgets were approved by the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) regional parliament based on informal, verbal “donations” of land secured from municipal and village elders. However, once construction equipment arrived, younger generations of heirs and adjacent clan claimants moved to halt paving operations, demanding compensation for the removal of thousands of mature rubber trees and coconut palms. The disputes have left some communities paying the price for unfinished roads. Most stalled projects are located in the interior areas of Sumisip, Tipo-Tipo, Tuburan, and Akbar. The absence of continuous paved routes has forced public transport drivers to charge double or triple the standard fares to cover vehicle damage caused by poor road conditions. For small-scale farmers, the higher transport costs consume much of their daily income. During downpours, unpaved sections become thick mud, isolating entire barangays and limiting residents’ access to emergency healthcare services. To address the issue, Cuevas said he has scheduled a meeting with contractors handling farm-to-market road projects across the province to discuss possible solutions to right-of-way problems. One of the most visible examples of the challenge is the Basilan Transcentral Road, where a dispute involving an estimated P18.5 million in compensation sought by local landowners has prevented the completion of about 8.5 kilometers of alternating dirt sections. Oversight data provided by Cuevas showed that key segments of the road, particularly mountain routes crossing the Sampinit Complex between Barangay Santa Clara in Lamitan City and Barangay Tumahubong in Sumisip, continue to face physical and legal obstacles. Despite significant funding releases from the BARMM regional parliament to complete the high-priority route, civil works on the final 8.5-kilometer stretch remain suspended. Tracking teams continue to encounter overlapping ancestral land claims, with clan heirs seeking a combined P18.5 million to cover land values and the replacement costs of thousands of high-yielding rubber trees scheduled for clearing. The BARMM public works ministry does not have flexible funds for property indemnity, leaving affected projects in the province indefinitely suspended. New law on right-of-way The problem in Basilan shows a broader challenge faced by infrastructure projects nationwide. During his 5th State of the Nation Address on Monday, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said the government has begun addressing persistent right-of-way disputes that have slowed project implementation, citing the 2025 Accelerated and Reformed Right-of-Way (ARROW) Act as a key measure to reduce delays. Signed into law in September 2025, the ARROW Act, or Republic Act No.12289 , amended existing right-of-way rules to streamline land acquisition for government infrastructure projects while maintaining safeguards for property owners, including the payment of just compensation. Marcos said that in the context of his administration’s efforts to expand and improve the country’s transport infrastructure, pointing out that such concerns had been among the major obstacles affecting mass transit projects. The new law, he said, should help fast-track land acquisition and project completion. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Groups say Marcos’ ‘predictive’ approach won’t fix disaster response gaps
articles.summary: CEBU, Philippines – Environmental groups and activists in the Visayas and Mindanao raised concerns over President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
articles.body: CEBU, Philippines – Environmental groups and activists in the Visayas and Mindanao raised concerns over President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s push for a “predictive” approach to disaster response, saying technology-driven systems must be paired with measures that address the challenges faced by communities when disasters disrupt basic services. In his fifth State of the Nation Address (SONA) on Monday, July 27, Marcos said the country has moved on from a reactive approach to disasters and is gearing toward a predictive, digitally-aided system of response. Environmental group Mindanao Climate Justice (MCJ) welcomed Marcos’ commitment to improving disaster response but said a digital-first approach alone could leave communities overlooked when power, communications, and transport networks fail. For Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (BAYAN) Central Visayas, Marcos’ predictive approach does not address what the group called the root problem in the country’s disaster prevention and response system: corruption . Marcos premised the government’s predictive disaster response approach on lessons learned from disasters in the Visayas and Mindanao, which resulted in the establishment of disaster resource centers and new response strategies. “Now, we’re not only proactive, but predictive as well, aided by digital tools. The strategies of public-private supply chains, hubs-and-spokes warehousing, automated production, and widescale pre-positioning of food and non-food supplies in LGUs, have proven their efficacy,” Marcos said during the SONA. Marcos said the government now has Mobile Energy Systems for communities needing emergency power, along with Government Emergency Communications Systems and private sector-led satellite-to-mobile services to maintain stable telecommunications during disasters. In a statement sent to Rappler on Tuesday, July 28, MCJ said, “Technology must support—not replace—community networks, accountable public institutions, and the leadership of affected Moro, Indigenous, and other local communities in planning and monitoring their recovery.” The group said poverty in communities also determines who are able to receive warnings, who are able to evacuate, whose homes are most vulnerable to disasters, and who remains displaced long after emergency assistance ends. “Families living on daily farming or informal work cannot rebuild through relief packs, tents, and emergency cash alone,” MCJ added. MCJ also urged Marcos to complete the promised primary disaster resource centers in Mindanao as soon as possible, citing the latest data from the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) that tallied displacement after the June 8 Mindanao earthquake at nearly 95,000 individuals. “A truly proactive response must continue through permanent housing, restored livelihoods, functioning schools and health services, psychosocial support, and safe and dignified return,” MCJ concluded. All must face accountability For its part, BAYAN Central Visayas called on the government to address first the problem on corruption. “Dili igo ang pag-preposition og relief goods kung ang gobyerno mismo napakyas sa pagpatuman og epektibong flood control ug disaster mitigation,” said BAYAN Central Visayas chairperson Jaime Paglinawan. (The pre-positioning of relief goods is not enough when the government itself failed to implement effective flood control and disaster mitigation.) BAYAN Central Visayas said the reported recovery of around P800 million and the freezing of several billion pesos that went to corruption were insignificant compared to the hundreds of billions in public funds that were used for anomalous flood control projects. It pointed out that the impact of disasters have been worsened by corruption, the destruction of natural resources, and policies that put big businesses and foreign powers first over the people’s welfare. “True predictive response means preventing the problem before disaster strikes, not waiting for the people to drown before acting. We must not allow the promises in the SONA to serve as a cover for the regime’s corruption and failure,” Paglinawan said. The group called for a broader investigation into all government officials and contractors allegedly involved in the flood control corruption scandal, rather than what it described as a limited probe into a few suspected individuals. During the SONA, Marcos named his close ally and cousin, former House speaker Martin Romualdez, saying he is set to face multiple cases to be filed by the Office of the Ombudsman. Earlier, the Ombudsman identified Romualdez as a central figure in the multibillion-peso flood control corruption scandal. Romualdez, in a statement on Monday afternoon, reiterated that he was ready to prove his innocence. Funds still needed While Marcos highlighted the government’s shift toward predictive disaster response, people in earthquake-hit provinces in Central Visayas and Soccsksargen continue to seek answers on the release of additional funds for disaster recovery. Marcos said the country has spent over P3 billion for immediate assistance to families who were most affected by the quakes — more than 600,000 based on the President Marcos’ count. Many parts of the recently-hit Sarangani province, General Santos City, and neighboring areas are still reeling from the impact of the June 2026 quake that caused P1.4-billion worth of damage to infrastructure. Likewise in Cebu, the September 2025 quake left the province with infrastructure damage of up to P73 million . On July 20, Sarangani Governor Rogelio “Ruel” Pacquiao disclosed that the province would be utilizing cash donations from private donors to cover repairs for over 1,500 damaged classrooms as the Department of Education “lacked the sufficient funds to repair them all.” On June 24, the Regional Development Council in Central Visayas approved a resolution asking national government agencies to expedite the release of P6.6 billion in rehabilitation funds for parts of Cebu that were hit by both the earthquake and Typhoon Tino (Kalmaegi) in 2025. According to the council, only P856 million has been released from an estimated P4.5 billion under the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Quick Response Fund meant for at least 148 repair and rehabilitation projects in Cebu. articles.title: [Vantage Point] Do you want to own one square meter of Ayala Avenue?
articles.summary: There is a simple way to understand tokenized securities, and it has nothing to do with Bitcoin.  Let’s say that you want to own a physical piece of a premium office tower on Ayala Avenue, valued at P20 billion.
articles.body: There is a simple way to understand tokenized securities, and it has nothing to do with Bitcoin. Let’s say that you want to own a physical piece of a premium office tower on Ayala Avenue, valued at P20 billion. Because a property like that is usually held by a big corporation or a real estate investment trust (REIT), your access to it will be restricted to purchasing listed shares or participating in institutional funds. But what if that same building could be digitally divided into millions of tiny ownership units, each representing a legally recognized fraction of the property? Instead of needing millions of pesos, an ordinary Filipino could invest a few thousand pesos and own a genuine economic interest in that asset. That is the basic idea behind tokenized securities, one of the innovations now being explored by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) under Chairperson Francis Lim through its Strategic Sandbox. In an exclusive interview, the SEC chairperson sought to demystify one of finance’s newest buzzwords. Despite its unfamiliar terminology, he explained, tokenization is not about creating another cryptocurrency. It is the use of blockchain technology to represent ownership of real-world financial assets in digital form under the supervision of securities regulators. Mainstream finance This matters because cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin derive their value largely from market demand and scarcity. A tokenized security, on the other hand, derives its value from an underlying asset that already exists. It could represent shares of stock, corporate bonds, government securities, real estate, infrastructure projects or even investment funds. The token is simply a new way of recording, transferring, and settling ownership. Think of it as replacing a paper land title with a secure digital title. The property does not change. It is only the method of proving ownership that becomes faster, cheaper, and more efficient. This idea is no longer theoretical. Singapore has become one of the world’s leaders through the Monetary Authority of Singapore’s Project Guardian, which brings together institutions such as DBS (Development Bank of Singapore), UBS (formerly known as Union Bank of Switzerland), JPMorgan, Citi, and Standard Chartered to test the tokenization of bonds, money market funds, foreign exchange transactions, and private credit. Rather than treating blockchain as a speculative technology, Singapore is integrating it into mainstream finance under clear regulatory rules. Switzerland has taken a similarly pragmatic approach. It established a legal framework that recognizes certain digital securities, allowing regulated financial institutions to issue and trade tokenized assets. Instead of replacing traditional financial markets, tokenization complements them by reducing paperwork, accelerating settlement times, and expanding market availability for investors. Even the United States, despite its cautious regulatory stance toward cryptocurrencies, has seen growing interest from major asset managers exploring tokenized money market funds, Treasury securities, and private investment products. Optimizing systems The direction is becoming increasingly clear. Global financial giants are not betting on cryptocurrencies replacing traditional finance. Instead, they are focused on using blockchain technology to optimize existing financial systems. The Philippines has every reason to pay attention. Our capital market has long suffered from a limited supply of investment products. Many Filipinos build wealth through bank deposits, real estate, or a relatively small number of listed stocks. Private companies often remain inaccessible to ordinary investors because minimum investment requirements are too high, while many infrastructure projects rely heavily on institutional capital. Tokenization has the potential to narrow those gaps. Imagine a solar power project costing P5 billion. Traditionally, financing would come from banks, institutional investors, or a public offering accessible mainly through conventional channels. Under a tokenized structure, that same project could theoretically be divided into millions of digital ownership units. A teacher investing P10,000, an overseas Filipino worker investing P25,000, and a retiree investing P50,000 could all participate in the same project through regulated digital securities. The same principle could eventually apply to warehouses, toll roads, commercial buildings, ports, and even private equity investments that have historically been reserved for wealthy investors. The real advantage is not that assets become cheaper. A P10-billion office building remains worth P10 billion. What changes is that ownership becomes divisible. Instead of buying an entire asset, investors buy precisely the portion they can afford. That seemingly simple change could dramatically broaden financial inclusion. There are operational benefits as well. Traditional securities transactions often involve multiple intermediaries, manual reconciliation, and settlement periods measured in days. Blockchain-based tokenization allows ownership records to be updated almost instantly, while maintaining an auditable record of every transaction. Administrative costs fall, settlement risk declines and markets become more efficient. Still, tokenization should not be romanticized. A tokenized security does not change its fundamental legal or financial nature. If the underlying company performs poorly, the token declines in value. If a commercial building loses tenants, investors suffer regardless of how ownership is recorded. Technology cannot eliminate credit risks or poor management. It simply modernizes the infrastructure through which investments are issued, traded, and settled. That is precisely why the SEC’s cautious approach deserves attention. Rather than rushing to approve every blockchain innovation, the commission has placed tokenized securities inside a regulatory sandbox where new products can be tested under supervision before wider adoption. The objective is not to chase technological fashion, but to understand how innovation can strengthen investor protection while expanding capital formation. Whether tokenization ultimately transforms Philippine finance remains uncertain. Many legal, tax, and operational issues still need to be resolved. Trading systems must evolve, custodial arrangements must be clarified, and investors must be educated. This is because technology advances far more quickly than the regulations governing it. Yet history suggests that financial markets continually evolve toward greater accessibility. Stock certificates gave way to electronic records. Trading floors gave way to online platforms. Paper checks gave way to digital payments. Each transition initially appeared unfamiliar until it became ordinary. Tokenized securities may represent the next chapter in that evolution. If implemented prudently, they could allow ordinary Filipinos to invest in assets that have traditionally been beyond their reach, not by making those assets smaller, but by making ownership more accessible. That may ultimately prove to be the most important innovation of all. I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future. articles.title: PH’s first liquid-fueled sounding rocket to be launched in 2027
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines will launch its first sounding rocket in Cagayan in 2027, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.  announced on Monday, July 27, paving the way for future space launch activities and a spaceport in Cagayan.  “A sounding rocket launch test is slated for next year.
articles.body: MANILA, Philippines – The Philippines will launch its first sounding rocket in Cagayan in 2027, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. announced on Monday, July 27, paving the way for future space launch activities and a spaceport in Cagayan. “A sounding rocket launch test is slated for next year. Yes, we are going to launch a rocket into space. This we will do in partnership with a South Korean aerospace company,” Marcos said in his fifth State of the Nation Address . Marcos made the announcement after he described Cagayan as “both geographically and economically primed to serve as our gateway to space and host the country’s first spaceport.” Philippine Space Agency (PhilSA) said in a press statement on Monday that the 2027 launch will be a “demonstration flight of a liquid-fueled rocket” that carries a two-kilogram payload and set to reach an altitude of at least five kilometers. “The test launch in Cagayan in 2027 will help advance the Philippines’ launch capabilities, develop Filipino expertise in rocket technologies, and prepare for future space launch activitiesm” PhilSA said. Sounding rockets usually last five to 20 minutes in space, according to the National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and are launched for scientific experiments. In 2023, the Philippines launched the TALA rocket which used both solid fuel and liquid oxidizer. Liquid rockets require a more complex design and build than solid-fueled ones. Play Video Future regional space leader? PhilSA Director General Gay Jane Perez doubled down on the Philippines’ prime position for space activities. The intention is to make the Philippines a regional space industry leader. “With the Pacific Ocean to its east and its proximity to the equator, the Philippines is well positioned for safe and secure rocket launch and recovery operations, helping reduce costs, improve launch efficiency, and create opportunities for future launch services,” Perez said. The PhilSA earlier deployed Diwata and Maya microsatellites into orbit from the International Space Station. The agency used these deployed microsatellites for environmental monitoring and post-disaster assessment. Perez said the Cagayan spaceport will be a “commercial-driven, government-enabled spaceport.” It will eventually be available for companies looking for a strategic venue for launching rockets. “That reliability is where the Philippines intends to compete, and it marks a shift in the country’s role in the regional space economy, from a user of space services to one that helps provide them,” said Perez. The first sounding rocket launch is a project of PhilSa, the Department of Information and Communications Technology, and Cagayan Economic Zone Authority, in partnership with Ascend International Gateway, Incorporated, and South Korea-based space mobility firm Perigee Aerospace Incorporated. articles.title: China accuses US of ‘AI hegemonism,’ threatens countermeasures over potential probes
articles.summary: BEIJING, China – China’s commerce ministry on Monday, July 27, accused the United States of “AI hegemonism” and threatened countermeasures after senior US officials said Chinese AI companies could face investigations, sanctions and trade restrictions over the alleged theft of US technology.
articles.body: BEIJING, China – China’s commerce ministry on Monday, July 27, accused the United States of “AI hegemonism” and threatened countermeasures after senior US officials said Chinese AI companies could face investigations, sanctions and trade restrictions over the alleged theft of US technology. The ministry said Washington was threatening Chinese companies with punishment based on allegations they used “distillation” to copy advanced US AI models, despite what it called a lack of factual or legal grounds. Model distillation is a widely used AI training technique in which developers use the outputs of a more capable model to train or improve another system. US officials say they distinguish between legitimate distillation and large-scale extraction that amounts to intellectual property theft. ‘All necessary measures’ “For any action that causes substantive harm to Chinese interests, China will take all necessary measures to firmly safeguard its legitimate rights and interests,” a ministry spokesperson said in a statement. The comments mark an escalation in a dispute centered on Beijing-based Moonshot AI, whose recently released Kimi K3 model has drawn attention for its coding capabilities and intensified debate in Washington over whether Chinese developers are copying US models or rapidly closing the technological gap through their own research. The controversy echoes the reaction in the US to the rise of Chinese startup DeepSeek last year. White House Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios said last week the US government had information indicating Moonshot distilled Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5 model to develop Kimi K3. Kratsios alleged Moonshot had built a sophisticated internal platform to conduct large-scale distillation of US models and switched between multiple methods of access to avoid detection. He also alleged the company had acquired servers equipped with Nvidia’s GB300 chips and accessed such systems in Thailand, likely to train its models. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent later warned that Chinese companies could face financial sanctions or placement on the Commerce Department’s Entity List, which restricts access to US technology. “We support open-source AI and the innovation it unlocks. But open source is not open season on American IP,” Bessent wrote on social media platform X. “When PRC (Chinese) firms conduct covert, industrial-scale distillation attacks that cross the line into IP theft, sanctions and Entity List designations will be on the table,” he said. Moonshot has rejected suggestions that Kimi K3’s performance was achieved via distillation, telling China’s National Business Daily last week that its performance gains came from original changes to underlying architecture. Placement on the Entity List could severely restrict Moonshot’s access to U.S. semiconductors, software and cloud services. The US used the trade blacklist as a central part of its campaign against Chinese telecommunications equipment maker Huawei beginning in 2019. Anthropic said in February it had identified more than 3.4 million interactions with its Claude models linked to Moonshot. It said hundreds of fraudulent accounts were used to target capabilities including reasoning, coding, data analysis, tool use, computer vision and the operation of computers. – Rappler.com

articles.body: MANILA, Philippines – The first Bangsamoro parliamentary election in September will be peaceful and credible, said President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Monday, July 27 – a promise to the Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) electorate that has waited long enough for the much-delayed polls. “Comelec, law enforcement, volunteers, deputized agencies, and all stakeholders are now ready to ensure that this defining political exercise will be peaceful, orderly, and credible,” Marcos said in his State of the Nation Address (SONA). Marcos called the election “a critical accomplishment under the Comprehensive Agreement on the Bangsamoro.” In the September polls, the Bangsamoro people will elect an 80-member parliament who will then select among themselves the new chief minister. The interim Bangsamoro government is currently led by Abdulraof Macacua who was present in Batasan during Marcos’ fifth SONA. Recently, the President appointed peace adviser Mel Senen Sarmiento as concurrent head of the government peace implementing panel with the Moro Islamic Liberation Front. For Commission on Elections (Comelec) Chairman George Garcia, the President’s mention of the Bangsamoro polls in the SONA signals that the election is set to finally take place in September. The election period and gun ban in the region officially started mid-July. ‘First in political history’ Marcos also touted in his SONA the awarded petroleum service contracts in the Bangsamoro which marks the first co-management service contracts in the country. “This is the first time in our political history,” Marcos said. “BARMM is now firmly set to pursue its strategic vision of energy security and total electrification for and in the Bangsamoro region.” The contracts cover areas in the Sulu Sea, according to the BARMM’s Ministry of Environment, Natural Resources, and Energy. “The winning service contractor is a four-way joint venture between an Australian company, a British company, and two Filipino-owned firms,” the ministry said . “Their partnership signals international trust in the promise of BARMM and its role in the Philippines’ sustainable development.” These are two out of the total 14 contracts the government awarded across the country. – Rappler.com
